key_gap: Both sides converged on the same ARR-protecting plan (fix sales comp and reseller margin first, repair the 2 burned accounts, migrate in waves sequenced by renewal risk, support surge per wave, target ≥ 95% ARR retention on the $9.5M legacy base), but the human produced the full stakeholder map first pass — want/capability/predicted-move rows for 8+ parties, deriving the perverse sales-comp incentive, the reseller margin channel (18% of affected revenue), the burned-trust accounts, the in-window renewals, and the competitor rescue play all from incentive logic. The AI found the comp perversity and renewals only through an explicit stakeholder pass inside WHY (a disclosed Phase-2 compensation in v5), and missed the reseller channel entirely until a HOW premortem exposed that 18% of the affected revenue had no counter-move in the plan; its sequencing was corrected from contract size to renewal risk during verification rather than at frame time.
learning_signal: For rollout and org-change decisions, the failure surface is stakeholder incentives, not engineering: run a mandatory first-pass inventory in which every party gets a want / capability / predicted-move row (customers, sales, channels, support, finance, competitors — not just 'the customer'), then hunt specifically for perverse incentives (comp plans, margin structures that reward the status quo) and derive hidden requirements from incentives rather than from the brief (renewal windows, burned trust, competitor rescue plays, support overload). Sequence the plan by stakeholder risk — who can block, who will be fought — before touching contract size, and give every predicted move a counter-move before any customer communication.
suggested_improvement: Promote the Phase-2 stakeholder compensation to a first-class stage: add a mandatory stakeholder pass immediately after WHAT for org-change/rollout tasks — (a) inventory with want/capability/predicted-move per party (including channels and competitor plays, which are commonly missed), (b) explicit perverse-incentive hunt (any party paid to preserve the status quo), (c) hidden-requirement probes (renewal windows, trust-debt accounts, capacity shortfalls), and (d) a check that every stakeholder's predicted move has a counter-move in the plan before HOW. This converts correct-but-late coverage (WHY self-check + HOW premortem) into first-pass discovery.

key_gap: The pure style hit its three registered failure modes simultaneously: stakeholder inflation (the inventory grew to 120 households, regulators, town businesses, future customers — none with a decision-relevant lever), paralysis by empathy (every affected party's pain vetoed the move, producing a 6-month 'stakeholder task force' and a bridge subsidy), and empathy substituting for the decision ('the social cost exceeds the financial gain' — keep the route). It never made a call and proposed a 6-month study that was physically impossible before the 60-day take-or-pay lock-in — by the time it reported, the fleet would be re-committed by default and the decision made for them; it also under-weighted that the urban-client threat (30% of revenue) was 3x the division's revenue. The AI separated decision right (owner alone) from impact (everyone else), treated the take-or-pay clause as the binding deadline, made the unilateral shutdown call within the 2-week window, and spent the empathy on the 90-day transition (severance, outplacement, town handoff) instead of the go/no-go.
learning_signal: Stakeholder analysis is a design tool, not an authorization tool: separate decision right (who decides) from impact (who is affected) at frame time, and bound stakeholder engagement by the calendar — hard deadlines (take-or-pay clauses, budget cycles, contract renewals) convert 'let's study more' into 'default decision by deadline expiry,' so consultation windows must close before the constraint binds. Empathy is an implementation input, not a decision criterion: the human cost is handled in the transition design (severance, continuity, outplacement), while the go/no-go rests on economics and the deadline. Keep every stakeholder whose lever cannot move the decision inside the window out of the weighted set.
suggested_improvement: Add a decision-right/deadline pre-check to META or WHAT for any decision task: (a) name the mandate holder and confirm no stakeholder holds veto; (b) list hard deadlines and compute the 'default decision' that occurs if no call is made by each deadline; (c) classify stakeholders as decide / input / informed and bound consultation to the earliest deadline; (d) route empathy explicitly to implementation design (transition, severance, continuity) while the go/no-go is evaluated on the decision right's criteria. Include a register failure-mode check: if the selected option is 'study more' or 'keep the status quo for humane reasons,' re-verify it against the deadline math and the mandate holder's criteria before accepting.
